title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: the promise and the proof

questions.prompt: A hotel advertisement printed these three promises, and no others: "A coach will take you straight to the hotel." · "Every room looks onto the gardens." · "A doctor is on call day and night." Which complaint is built on something the advertisement really promised?

options.text: You said that a coach would take us straight to the hotel, and we waited for a taxi.
You said that every room had a balcony, and ours looked out on a blank wall.
You said that the doctor's visits were free, and we were billed for the one we needed.
You said that there was a night porter, and the front desk was empty at midnight.

questions.explanation: A complaint is only as strong as the promise it reports, and the advertisement will be lying on the counter between you. The coach was promised and no coach came, so the report is faithful and the complaint holds. A room that looks onto the gardens is not a room with a balcony. A doctor on call day and night is a promise about when he can be reached, never about what he charges. And a night porter was not mentioned at all. Stretch a promise and you hand the argument back to the agency.

questions.prompt: Marion's vouchers had still not arrived, so she rang the agency on Friday. Afterwards she wrote down what the agent had told her: "He said that he had posted the vouchers the week before and that he would call the hotel that afternoon." Which words did the agent actually use?

options.text: I had posted the vouchers the week before, and I would call the hotel that afternoon.
I posted the vouchers last week, and I will call the hotel this afternoon.
I have posted the vouchers this week, and I am calling the hotel right now.
I will post the vouchers next week, and I called the hotel this morning.

questions.explanation: Recovering the exact words means undoing every move: would comes forward to will, the week before comes back to last week, that afternoon to this afternoon, and the reporter's he becomes the speaker's I. The past perfect had posted could come from a past simple or from a present perfect, and it is the time marker that decides: the week before points to last week, so the agent's own verb was posted and not have posted this week. Keeping the report's tenses inside quotation marks quotes nobody at all, and pushing the posting into next week while the call is already over turns both events round.

questions.prompt: Marion's letter of complaint mixes two kinds of sentence. Tick EVERY sentence in which she reports a promise the agency made — not a fact about her holiday.

options.text: You told me that the price included all the airport taxes.
We arrived at two in the morning after a nine-hour flight.
You said that the new wing would be finished before the season.
The building site beside the pool started work at seven.
You promised us a room with a view of the sea.

questions.explanation: A reported promise is recognised first by its reporting verb, whose subject is the agency: you told me, you said, you promised. Behind two of them stand words the agency once pronounced, stepped back into the past — included and would be finished are the backshifted forms of includes and will be finished; the third names the promise instead of quoting it, and holds the agency just as firmly. The two remaining sentences have no reporting verb at all: they are Marion's own account of what happened, and they belong to the second move of a complaint, where you state the facts. A complaint needs both kinds, but only the promises can be held against the agency.

questions.prompt: At the desk, the agent answers Marion's two complaints: "I do apologise for the transfer, madam. But I have your booking form here, and the excursions were never part of your package." One of the two halves has just been conceded to her. Which answer presses that half?

options.text: I am quite certain that the excursions were mentioned when I booked.
Then I suppose there is nothing more to be said, and I will go.
Thank you for that. What do you intend to do about the transfer?
I would like to speak to somebody more senior than you, please.

questions.explanation: An answer of this kind often makes two moves at once, and the hinge is the little word but: whatever follows it names what the agency will not pay for. The apology covers the transfer and nothing else, so that is the half already conceded and the half worth pressing, and a precise question about what he now intends to do keeps him on ground he has given up. Arguing that the excursions were mentioned attacks the half he has just documented, with the booking form lying on the counter between you. Announcing that there is nothing more to be said hands back the concession he made. And asking for a more senior person changes the listener without moving the complaint one step.

questions.prompt: A guest said at the desk: "The pool was closed all week, and I am not at all happy about it." Three of these reports only repeat her words. Which one also passes on her annoyance?

options.text: She complained that the pool had been closed all week.
She said that the pool had been closed all week.
She told the manager that the pool had been closed all week.
She added that the pool had been closed all week.

questions.explanation: Say and tell hand on the words and nothing else: a reader given only she said, or she told the manager, learns what the pool was doing and not what the guest was feeling. To complain is to hand on the words together with the dissatisfaction behind them, and it is the verb your own lesson keeps for exactly this move. To add brings in a further point in a list, and there is nothing here for it to be added to. Choosing a verb that carries the force is what turns a transformation exercise into real writing.

questions.prompt: The agent offers: "We can't refund the trip, but I can give you a 20 % discount on your next holiday with us." Marion answers: "I'm afraid I won't be booking another holiday with your agency." What does her answer mean?

options.text: she accepts the offer but wants to pay even less next time
she refuses the offer, because it would buy her nothing
she is asking the agent to explain his discount once again
she apologises for having complained about her holiday

questions.explanation: I'm afraid announces a polite refusal, and the rest of the sentence explains why the offer is empty: a discount is money off a holiday she has already decided never to buy. Refusing compensation is not haggling over its size, and nothing in her answer asks a question. As for the apology, I'm afraid only sounds like one: it is the soft padding English lays under bad news.
